# Session 9: How a Neural Network Learns, and Why Training Fails

## Learning goals

By the end of this session you should be able to:

- describe the training cycle (predictions → loss → gradients → update) and write the standard PyTorch training loop;
- explain backpropagation as the chain rule applied from the loss backwards through the network;
- choose the loss for classification (cross-entropy) and regression (mean squared error), and explain why confident mistakes are expensive;
- recognize three common ways training fails (equal starting weights, vanishing gradients, a poor optimizer or learning rate) and name the fix for each;
- judge when a hidden layer pays off, and why a very large network can lose to a simple baseline;
- use early stopping, weight decay and dropout against overfitting, and evaluate the result honestly.

Sessions 7, 8 and 9 form one progression. Session 7 asked **what a neural network can represent**. Session 8 asked **how we know whether a model generalizes**. This session asks **how we actually train a network, and why training sometimes succeeds and sometimes fails**.

The starting point is concrete. In Session 8 we built a network, but its weights were random, so its predictions were no better than chance. We had labelled examples, so how do we turn the random weights into useful predictions? Here, we try to answers that question. We will be using four different datasets: breast-cancer biopsies (the training loop), a protein fitness landscape (why training fails, and when a hidden layer pays off), Session 8's protein localization (when a network is too large for its data), and MNIST digits in the lab.

## From an untrained network to a trained network {#sec-s09-trained}

The **Wisconsin breast-cancer** dataset has 569 fine-needle biopsies, each described by 30 features measured on microscope images of the cell nuclei (radius, texture, perimeter, smoothness, concavity and so on). Each biopsy is labelled malignant (212) or benign (357). We split it into 398 training, 85 validation and 86 test biopsies, and standardize the features with statistics from the training set only (Session 8). The network has one hidden layer of 16 ReLU units and one output, 513 weights in all.

Training repeats one cycle, over and over:

![The training cycle. The network turns inputs into predictions; the loss measures how wrong they are compared with the labels; backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight; the optimizer updates the weights. The same five lines of PyTorch (right) do this for every mini-batch, in every epoch.](figs/session09-training-cycle.png){width="100%"}

Before training, the network's predicted probabilities all sit close to 0.5: it is guessing (validation accuracy 0.659, roughly the share of benign biopsies). After 100 passes through the training data, the benign biopsies are pushed towards 0 and the malignant ones towards 1:

![Left: training and validation loss per epoch. Both fall quickly; after about 50 epochs the validation loss stops improving while the training loss keeps falling, and we keep the weights from the epoch with the lowest validation loss (early stopping). Right: predicted probability of malignancy for the 85 validation biopsies, before and after training.](figs/session09-bc-training.png){width="100%"}

On the test set the trained network reaches accuracy 0.953, MCC 0.900 and AUROC 0.984: 2 benign biopsies called malignant and 2 malignant ones missed.

**Was the hidden layer needed?** Not here. Compared by 5-fold cross-validation (one test split of 86 biopsies is too noisy, Session 8), logistic regression with 31 weights and the network with 513 both reach an accuracy of **0.979**. Malignant and benign nuclei differ mainly in size and shape, and a weighted sum of those measurements already separates them. Training works; the extra capacity simply has nothing to add. @sec-s09-epistasis shows a dataset where it does.

## How backpropagation finds every gradient {#sec-s09-backprop}

Gradient descent (Session 1, Session 7) needs $\partial L / \partial w$, the slope of the loss, for **every** weight. For a single layer that was easy. But what about a weight buried several layers inside a network, whose effect on the loss passes through every later layer?

![A tiny network: two inputs, one tanh hidden unit $h$, one sigmoid output $\hat y$, and the loss $L$. The forward pass (grey) computes the prediction and the loss. The backward pass (red) applies the chain rule from the loss back towards the inputs: $\partial L/\partial \hat y$ is computed once and reused for $w_3$, then multiplied by $\partial \hat y/\partial h$ and reused for $w_1$ and $w_2$.](figs/session09-backprop.png){width="90%"}

**Backpropagation is an efficient application of the chain rule, from the loss backwards through the network.** Each layer's "error signal" is computed once and reused for all the weights feeding into it, so the cost of all the gradients is about the same as one forward pass. Without that reuse, networks with thousands or millions of weights could not be trained.

You do not have to differentiate networks by hand. The notebook does it once for the tiny network above (five gradients, worked out with the chain rule), then builds the same network in PyTorch and calls `loss.backward()`: all five gradients agree to eight decimal places. From then on, PyTorch's **autograd** does it for any network.

That gives the **training loop** you will write yourself in the lab:

``` python
for epoch in range(n_epochs):
    for xb, yb in loader:                 # one mini-batch at a time
        optimizer.zero_grad()             # 1. clear the old gradients
        logits = model(xb)                # 2. forward pass
        loss = criterion(logits, yb)      # 3. how wrong is it?
        loss.backward()                   # 4. backpropagation: every gradient
        optimizer.step()                  # 5. update every weight
```

Real training uses **mini-batches**: a `DataLoader` shuffles the training set every epoch and serves it in small batches (here 32 biopsies), and the weights are updated after every batch. That gives many cheap, slightly noisy steps per **epoch** (one pass through the training data) instead of one expensive exact step; this is **stochastic gradient descent**. After every epoch we measure the validation loss and keep the best weights (**early stopping**).

## Which loss to minimize {#sec-s09-loss}

The loss decides what "wrong" means. For **regression** we use the **mean squared error** between prediction and target. For **classification** we use **cross-entropy**. For one example it is the negative log of the probability the model gave the true class,

$$
\text{CE} = -\log p(\text{true class}),
$$

its *surprise* in the language of Session 1. Averaged over a dataset, it is the negative log-likelihood, so minimizing it is maximum likelihood (Session 1).

![Cross-entropy as a function of the probability given to the true class. A confident correct answer costs almost nothing; a confident mistake costs a lot.](figs/session09-cross-entropy.png){width="60%"}

Confidently wrong is punished far more than hedging: probability 0.9 on the truth costs 0.105, probability 0.01 costs 4.6, over 40 times more. This is what pushes a classifier to separate the classes, as in the right panel of the breast-cancer figure. For two classes PyTorch's `nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss`, and for more classes `nn.CrossEntropyLoss`, combine the sigmoid or log-softmax with this loss in one numerically stable step, so the model outputs raw logits (Session 8). The notebook checks both by hand. The lab compares cross-entropy with mean squared and mean absolute error for the same digit classifier: cross-entropy trains best.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Optional: cross-entropy and relative entropy

Cross-entropy is built from the relative entropy (Kullback-Leibler divergence) of Session 4: $H(P, Q) = H(P) + D_{\text{KL}}(P \| Q)$, the true distribution's own entropy plus the extra cost of describing it with the model's distribution $Q$. Since $H(P)$ does not depend on the model, minimizing cross-entropy is minimizing the KL divergence between the model's predictions and the true labels.
:::

## Why training fails {#sec-s09-failures}

The training loop always runs; it does not always learn. Here are three common failures, each shown by changing one thing in a network that predicts the fitness of protein variants (the GB1 data of @sec-s09-epistasis: 20,000 training variants, each described by the one-hot encoding of four residues). We measure the validation error as the mean absolute error (MAE) of the predicted $\log_{10}$ fitness. Predicting the training mean for every variant gives an MAE of 0.488; a working 64/64 network reaches 0.250 within 20 epochs.

![Four experiments. (1) Gradient size per layer in a freshly initialized network with six hidden layers: with sigmoid, the first layer receives about ten million times less gradient than the last. (2) Starting every weight at the same value. (3) Six hidden layers with sigmoid, tanh or ReLU, trained with plain gradient descent (SGD), and sigmoid trained with Adam. (4) Optimizer and learning rate. The dotted line is the error of predicting the mean.](figs/session09-training-failures.png){width="100%"}

### Failure 1: every weight starts the same

- **Observation.** Start all weights at 0.1 instead of small random numbers. After 20 epochs the validation MAE is 0.352, little better than the additive (linear) model's 0.371, against 0.250 from a random start.
- **Why?** Every hidden unit computes the same thing and receives the same gradient, so the units stay identical for ever. After training, all 64 units in the first layer are still exactly the same: 64 units behave like one.
- **Fix.** Random initialization *breaks the symmetry*. PyTorch does this by default.

### Failure 2: deep sigmoid networks, and vanishing gradients

- **Observation.** A network with six hidden layers of sigmoid units, trained with plain SGD, does not learn at all: its validation MAE stays around 0.48, the error of predicting the mean. The same network with tanh (0.321) or ReLU (0.312) learns.
- **Why?** Backpropagation multiplies one activation *derivative* per layer, and sigmoid's derivative is at most 0.25 (and almost 0 when the unit saturates). Even in the best case, six layers multiply the gradient by $0.25^6 \approx 0.00024$, so the first layer gets at least 4,000 times less gradient than the last. In practice it is worse: most units are not at the steepest point, and the weights shrink the gradient further. In a freshly initialized six-layer sigmoid network, the first layer's gradient is about **ten million times smaller** than the last layer's; for tanh and ReLU the ratio is a few hundred to two thousand. The first layers barely move.
- **Fix.** ReLU-like activations; initialization scaled to each layer's size; standardized inputs; normalization layers such as batch normalization (Ioffe & Szegedy, 2015); and modern architectures. Adaptive optimizers also help: the same sigmoid network trained with Adam, which rescales small gradients ([see below](#sec-s09-adam)), does learn (0.291).

![Derivatives of sigmoid, tanh and ReLU. Sigmoid's is at most 0.25 (at $z = 0$) and below 0.01 by $|z| = 6$. Tanh's peaks at 1 but also vanishes in both tails. ReLU's is exactly 0 or exactly 1.](figs/session09-activation-derivatives.png){width="65%"}

ReLU never shrinks the gradient for positive inputs and is cheap to compute, so it is the default for hidden layers. Its weakness is the flat side: a unit whose input is negative for every example gets no gradient and never recovers ("dying ReLU"; the first discussion problem). **Leaky ReLU** and **GELU** keep a small slope there. Sigmoid remains standard for a binary *output*.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### The same problem comes back, three more times

Whenever a gradient has to pass through many multiplications, it can vanish (or explode). You will meet it again:

- **Very deep CNNs (Session 10).** Even with ReLU and batch normalization, plain networks deeper than about 20 layers trained *worse* than shallower ones. ResNet (2015) added **residual connections**: each block adds its output to its input, $x + f(x)$, so the signal and the gradient always have a direct path through the network.
- **Recurrent networks (Session 11).** An RNN applies the same weights at every position, so the gradient is multiplied by the same factor once per step through the sequence. **LSTM** gates were invented to give it a protected path.
- **Transformers (Session 11).** Dozens of blocks deep, they use residual connections and layer normalization in every block, for the same reason.
:::

### Failure 3: the optimizer and the learning rate

- **Observation.** The same 64/64 network reaches a validation MAE of 0.250 with Adam (learning rate 0.001), but only 0.305 with plain SGD in the same 20 epochs. With Adam and a learning rate of 0.1, the error jumps around and never gets below 0.298.
- **Why?** The learning rate sets the step size of gradient descent (Session 1). Too small is slow; too large overshoots the minimum. Adam averages the recent gradients and adapts the step size for each weight; the next subsection explains why that helps.
- **Fix.** Start with Adam and a learning rate around $10^{-3}$, and always watch the validation curve.

### Momentum and Adam: why an optimizer can beat plain SGD {#sec-s09-adam}

Plain SGD takes each step straight down the gradient of the current mini-batch, with the same learning rate for every weight. That works badly when the loss surface is a long, narrow valley, which is common in networks because some weights affect the loss far more than others. The gradient then points mostly *across* the valley: a learning rate large enough to make progress *along* the valley makes SGD zigzag from wall to wall or blow up, and a safe one crawls along the valley floor. Two ideas fix this.

- **Momentum.** Step along a running average of the recent gradients instead of the latest one, like a heavy ball rolling downhill. Across the valley, successive gradients point in opposite directions and cancel; along the valley they agree and add up. Averaging also smooths out the noise of individual mini-batches.
- **A step size for each weight.** Divide each weight's step by the typical size of its own recent gradients. A weight whose gradients are tiny (the gentle direction of the valley, or an early layer of a deep sigmoid network) gets a larger step; a weight whose gradients are large gets a smaller one.

**Adam** (Kingma & Ba, 2015) combines the two. For every weight it keeps an average of the gradient $g$ (the momentum, $m$) and an average of $g^2$ ($s$, which measures the gradient's typical size), and updates

$$m \leftarrow \beta_1 m + (1-\beta_1)\,g, \qquad s \leftarrow \beta_2 s + (1-\beta_2)\,g^2, \qquad w \leftarrow w - \eta\,\frac{m}{\sqrt{s} + \epsilon}$$

with $\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 = 0.999$ and a tiny $\epsilon$ that avoids dividing by zero (Adam also corrects $m$ and $s$ for starting at zero). Because $m/\sqrt{s}$ is roughly $\pm 1$ when the gradients are consistent, every weight moves by about the learning rate $\eta$, whatever the scale of its gradient. That is why one default, $\eta = 10^{-3}$, works for many networks, and why Adam rescued the deep sigmoid network of Failure 2.

![Three optimizers on a valley that is 100 times steeper across ($w_2$) than along ($w_1$), 60 steps each. SGD, with the largest learning rate it tolerates, first zigzags across the valley and then crawls along it (loss 0.09 after 60 steps). Momentum (loss 0.0004) and Adam (0.006) both reach the minimum. Adam heads for it from the first step, because it takes equal steps in both directions.](figs/session09-optimizers.png){width="100%"}

Adam is a good default, not a law. In the figure, well-tuned momentum ends even lower than Adam, and for some image networks plain SGD with momentum still generalizes slightly better. On the GB1 network, Adam reached a validation MAE of 0.250 against 0.305 for plain SGD in the same 20 epochs. The lab asks you to run this comparison yourself and explain the result.

The lab repeats all of these on the blood-cell images of the Session 8 lab, and adds the comparison of loss functions: *change one thing, see what happens, explain why*.

## When a hidden layer pays off: epistasis in a protein {#sec-s09-epistasis}

**The data.** GB1 is a small domain of protein G, a bacterial protein that binds antibodies (IgG). Wu et al. (2016) made all 20⁴ = 160,000 combinations of amino acids at four of its positions (V39, D40, G41 and V54), and measured by deep sequencing how well each variant binds IgG; 149,361 variants have a value. Fitness is relative to the wild type (VDGV = 1) and spans several orders of magnitude, so we predict $\log_{10}(\text{fitness} + 0.001)$. Each variant is described by the **one-hot encoding** of its four residues (Session 7): 4 × 20 = 80 numbers.

**Additive or not?** A linear model on this encoding gives every amino acid at every position its own weight, and adds them up. It is an **additive** model, exactly like a profile or PSSM (Session 5): each position contributes on its own. It cannot represent **epistasis**, where the effect of a mutation depends on which residues sit at the other positions. That is the non-additive, XOR-like pattern of Session 7, now as a measured property of a real protein. A hidden layer can represent it.

Trained with early stopping on 20,000 variants (5,000 for validation, 20,000 for testing):

| Model                       | Weights | Train MAE | Val MAE | Test MAE | **Test** $R^2$ |
|-----------------------------|---------|-----------|---------|----------|----------------|
| Linear (additive)           | 81      | 0.379     | 0.371   | 0.385    | **0.496**      |
| 64/64                       | 9,409   | 0.212     | 0.250   | 0.254    | **0.787**      |
| 64/64 + weight decay (10⁻³) | 9,409   | 0.215     | 0.241   | 0.249    | 0.795          |
| 64/64 + dropout 0.2         | 9,409   | 0.220     | 0.242   | 0.247    | 0.798          |
| 256/256                     | 86,785  | 0.193     | 0.252   | 0.259    | 0.779          |

![Training (dashed) and validation (solid) MAE per epoch, for the additive model and the 64/64 network.](figs/session09-gb1-curves.png){width="70%"}

The network explains about 79% of the variance in fitness, against 50% for the additive model. Weight decay and dropout help a little, and a network ten times larger does not help further.

![Left and middle: predicted against measured $\log_{10}$ fitness for the 20,000 test variants (colour: how many variants fall in each hexagon). The additive model compresses the predictions into a narrow band and misses the fit variants; the network follows the diagonal. Right: test $R^2$ against the number of training variants.](figs/session09-gb1-epistasis.png){width="100%"}

**The network needs data to learn the interactions.** With 500 training variants the two models are equally good ($R^2$ 0.43 against 0.41): the interactions exist, but there are too few examples to learn them. From a few thousand variants on, the network pulls away (0.72 at 5,000, 0.82 at 60,000), while the additive model is stuck at about 0.49, however much data it gets: no amount of data lets a sum represent an interaction.

This is Session 7's lesson on real biological data: a hidden layer can represent non-additive relationships, and with enough data, training actually finds them. It is also the limitation of profiles noted in Session 5: a sum over positions cannot capture interactions. Session 12 returns to it with pairwise models learned from multiple alignments. The second discussion problem asks where the advantage comes from, by giving the linear model hand-made interaction features for each pair of positions, as Session 7 did for XOR with $x_1 x_2$.

## Why not make the network enormous? {#sec-s09-enormous}

If larger networks can represent more, why not always use an enormous one? Session 8's protein-localization network answers that. It has 3000 inputs (150 residues, one-hot), a hidden layer of 64 units and 5 outputs: **192,389 weights**, trained on only **486 proteins** of the homology-aware split.

![Training and validation accuracy of the localization network per epoch. Training accuracy reaches 1.0 within a few epochs; validation accuracy peaks at 0.486 (epoch 5) and then falls.](figs/session09-localization-overfitting.png){width="65%"}

Training accuracy reaches **1.000**: the network memorizes every training protein. Validation accuracy peaks at **0.486** after five epochs and then *falls*, to 0.438 by epoch 29. This is **overfitting** in its plainest form: with far more freedom than data, the network learns the idiosyncrasies of the training sequences instead of the general signal.

And the simple baseline wins. Measured once on the test set:

| Metric | Untrained network (Session 8, val) | Trained network (test) | Logistic regression (test) |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Accuracy | 0.181 | 0.514 | **0.569** |
| Macro F1 | 0.124 | 0.493 | — |
| MCC | −0.027 | 0.394 | **0.461** |
| Macro AUROC | 0.474 | 0.831 | **0.849** |

Training works, since every number is far above chance. But **the linear model is better**. Always compare against a simple baseline before believing that a bigger model is better.

## What can we do about overfitting? {#sec-s09-overfitting}

- **More data.** The most reliable fix, and often the only one that really helps.
- **A smaller model, or a better architecture.** Fewer weights for the same input. Session 10's convolutional network needs 19,237 weights instead of 192,389.
- **Early stopping.** Keep the weights from the epoch with the best validation score. It costs nothing and is used throughout this course.
- **Weight decay (L2) and L1 regularization.** Add a penalty for large weights to the loss ([below](#sec-s09-l1l2)).
- **Dropout.** Randomly switch off a fraction of the units in every training step, so the network cannot rely on any single unit.

Applied to the localization network, dropout and weight decay do *not* beat early stopping alone (best validation accuracy 0.476 against 0.486). Training accuracy still reaches 1.000 whatever we do: with 192,389 weights and 486 examples the network can always memorize. Regularization is not a substitute for enough data.

### Penalizing large weights: L2 and L1 {#sec-s09-l1l2}

A network that fits noise usually does it with some very large weights: a big weight makes the output jump when one input changes a little. Regularization adds a penalty for large weights to the loss, with a strength $\lambda$ that we choose on the validation set:

$$
\text{loss} = \text{cross-entropy} + \lambda \sum_j w_j^2 \quad\text{(L2)} \qquad\text{or}\qquad \text{cross-entropy} + \lambda \sum_j |w_j| \quad\text{(L1)}
$$

- **L2** pulls every weight towards zero in proportion to its size (the gradient of $\lambda w^2$ is $2\lambda w$). Every step therefore shrinks every weight by the same *fraction*, which is why it is called **weight decay** and why PyTorch implements it as the optimizer's `weight_decay` argument. Weights become small, but almost never exactly zero.
- **L1** pulls with the same force, $\lambda$, however small a weight already is. Weights that help little are pushed all the way to **exactly zero**, so the model *selects features*.

For linear regression the two have their own names, **ridge** (L2) and **lasso** (L1). The notebook fits both to the 30 features of the breast-cancer biopsies of @sec-s09-trained, with logistic regression, so that every feature has exactly one weight:

![Logistic regression on the 30 biopsy features. Left and middle: every line is one feature's weight as the penalty gets stronger (to the right). Right: the number of non-zero weights (solid) and the validation accuracy (dotted).](figs/session09-l1-l2.png){width="100%"}

With $\lambda$ chosen on the validation set, L2 keeps all 30 weights (test accuracy 0.965), while L1 keeps only **6** (test accuracy 0.942), led by the largest tumour radius and the number of concave points on the cell nuclei: almost the same accuracy, with a model a pathologist can read. When features are many and examples few, as in gene-expression data with 20,000 genes and a few hundred patients, that is often the main reason to use L1. The third discussion problem checks the same effect by hand.

## Is the improvement real? {#sec-s09-real}

Session 8's rules apply to every comparison in this session: choices (epochs, sizes, regularization) are made on the validation set, the test set is used once, and every model is compared with a simple baseline. The three datasets side by side:

| Dataset | Training examples | Network weights | Examples per weight | Network vs. linear |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| Breast cancer | 398 | 513 | 0.78 | tie (CV accuracy 0.979 vs. 0.979) |
| GB1 fitness | 20,000 | 9,409 | 2.1 | **network** (test $R^2$ 0.787 vs. 0.496) |
| Protein localization | 486 | 192,389 | 0.003 | **linear** (test accuracy 0.514 vs. 0.569) |

- **Breast cancer:** the network trains well, but a linear model is just as good; the problem is nearly additive.
- **GB1 fitness:** the network clearly wins; the relationship is non-additive (epistasis), and there are enough data to learn it.
- **Protein localization:** the network memorizes and loses to the baseline; the data are scarce relative to the model.

Examples per weight is a **warning sign, not a strict rule**: modern networks often have more weights than training examples and still generalize, thanks to their architecture, regularization and the way they are trained. But when a model is huge relative to its data, check it against a baseline before trusting it.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
### Now you can read the whole PHD pipeline

Rost & Sander's PHD (1993, Session 7) is the recipe of Sessions 5-9 at the scale that mattered historically: **profile input** from a multiple alignment (Session 5), networks with a **hidden layer** (Session 7) and **three outputs** (Session 8), trained by **backpropagation** (this session), and evaluated by cross-validation on test sets purged of similar sequences (Session 8's homology partitioning). It reached 70.8% three-state accuracy.
:::

**Next: fewer weights, by using the structure of the data.** A fully connected layer has a separate weight for every connection, which is why the localization network needs 192,389 of them. A sequence, however, has structure: the same motif means the same thing wherever it occurs. Can we exploit that, and use far fewer weights? That is **convolution**, Session 10.

### Further reading

- Wikipedia, [Backpropagation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backpropagation), [Stochastic gradient descent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_gradient_descent) (including momentum and Adam), [Vanishing gradient problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanishing_gradient_problem), [Overfitting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overfitting), [Regularization (mathematics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regularization_(mathematics)), [Dropout (neural networks)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(neural_networks)), [Early stopping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_stopping)
- d2l.ai, [Multilayer Perceptrons](https://d2l.ai/chapter_multilayer-perceptrons/index.html)
- Ioffe & Szegedy (2015), [Batch Normalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.03167)
- Kingma & Ba (2015), [Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6980); d2l.ai, [Optimization Algorithms](https://d2l.ai/chapter_optimization/index.html) (momentum, Adam and others, with interactive examples)
- Rost & Sander (1993), [Prediction of protein secondary structure at better than 70% accuracy](https://doi.org/10.1006/jmbi.1993.1413), *J. Mol. Biol.* 232:584-599
- UCI Machine Learning Repository, [Breast Cancer Wisconsin (Diagnostic)](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/17/breast+cancer+wisconsin+diagnostic)

## The notebook

`notebooks/session09-backprop-training-regularization.ipynb` computes every number and figure on this page, section by section: the breast-cancer training run and the predictions before and after training; the backpropagation example by hand, checked against autograd; cross-entropy by hand; the three training failures (equal initialization, deep sigmoid networks, optimizer and learning rate); the GB1 models and the effect of the training-set size; and the localization network's overfitting, regularization and comparison with logistic regression.

Open it in [Google Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/ElofssonLab/kb8029-book/blob/main/notebooks/session09-backprop-training-regularization.ipynb) via the badge at the top of the notebook page to edit and run it yourself.

## The lab

**Full lab, on blood-cell images** (BloodMNIST, as in the Session 8 lab): adapted from the previous course's "Neural Networks" lab and rebuilt in PyTorch. This time you **write the training loop yourself**. Work through [`notebooks/session09-lab.ipynb`](https://colab.research.google.com/github/ElofssonLab/kb8029-book/blob/main/notebooks/session09-lab.ipynb), replacing every `todo(...)` call with your own code:

1.  write the four-step mini-batch training loop;
2.  compare cross-entropy with mean squared and mean absolute error as the loss for a classifier;
3.  start every weight at 1 and see why random initialization matters;
4.  add hidden layers (tanh, sigmoid, ReLU) and measure the gradient that reaches the first layer;
5.  compare plain SGD, SGD with momentum and Adam, a 128-unit hidden layer with no hidden layer at all, and run a small hyperparameter search chosen on the validation set, using the test set once, at the end.

The best dense network ends up near 78% on the test images. Session 10's lab trains a convolutional network on the same cells.

## What's next

Session 10 moves from fully connected networks to **convolutional** ones, which share weights across positions. It covers image classification and the ImageNet history, data augmentation and transfer learning (including breast-cancer histopathology images), the localization dataset again, now with 10 times fewer weights, DNA sequence (DeepSEA), and protein contact prediction.
